# Effects

Figma: [Effects](https://www.figma.com/design/a7Z956YZy9n6f9uz5DK16Y?node-id=69-883)

Visual treatments applied on top of base shapes - border radius, border colors, and shadow elevation. Each sub-system is governed by variables (radius/*, border/*) or effect styles (Shadow / *) backed by primitives. Designers compose interfaces from semantic tokens, not raw values.

## Effects Overview

Effects are visual treatments applied on top of base shapes. Syntropy provides three governed effect systems: border radius, border colors, and shadow elevation. Each is built on the same pattern as Color and Typography - semantic tokens that reference primitives, so designers never touch raw values.

- Border Radius - 11 semantic tokens covering corner rounding from sharp (none) to fully circular (full)
- Border Color - 16 semantic tokens covering default, brand, status, focus, and disabled states
- Shadow / Elevation - 6 effect styles (none, xs, sm, md, lg, xl); every level pairs an ambient and a key shadow to build the elevation hierarchy

> **Info:** Effects are applied differently from colors. Border radius binds to a node's cornerRadius property. Border color binds to strokes. Shadows are applied via effect styles, which are referenced by name (Shadow / md) rather than via variables - Figma handles shadows through its Effect system, not the variable system.

## Border Radius

The radius scale runs from none (sharp corners) to full (perfectly round). Each step is a meaningful jump - designers pick the closest fit rather than custom values. Most fintech UI uses sm or md for cards and inputs, lg for prominent surfaces, and full for avatars and circular buttons.

## Border Color

Border tokens follow the same naming pattern as text and icon tokens. Default for most surfaces, subtle for dividers, strong for emphasized boundaries, brand for branded outlines, status colors for state-driven boundaries, and focus for accessibility focus rings.

### Foundation

| border/default Most cards, inputs, modals | border/subtle Dividers, table rows, very light separation | border/strong Emphasized boundaries, hovered cards | border/disabled Disabled inputs and controls | border/inverse Borders on dark surfaces | border/focus Focus rings - see accessibility | border/progress Progress bar tracks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

### Brand

| border/brand/subtle Lightest brand outline | border/brand/muted Soft brand outline | border/brand/primary Standard brand outline | border/brand/accent Stronger brand outline | border/brand/darkest Darkest brand outline |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |

### Status

| border/success Success state outlines | border/warning Warning state outlines | border/error Error state outlines | border/info Info state outlines |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

## Shadow & Elevation

Five elevation levels (xs → xl) plus none form the shadow scale. Each level is built from two layers, following the Fluent model: an ambient shadow, soft and directionless, that implies how far the object sits from the surface, and a key shadow, sharper and offset downward, that defines the object's edge and implies a single light source above. The key layer follows blur = n and offsetY = n ÷ 2, a relationship the primitives already encode: Shadow/Blur/XS→XL is 2/4/8/16/32 against Shadow/OffsetY/XS→XL at 1/2/4/8/16. Low levels (xs, sm, md) take a 2px ambient blur; high levels (lg, xl) take 8px, so distant objects read as further away. Every radius, offset and colour binds to a Primitive Core variable, so adjusting a primitive updates every shadow. Apply only via the effect-style picker, never raw values.

### Key and ambient shadows

Key shadow: sharp and directional. Its blur equals the level's n and it offsets down by n ÷ 2, so it draws a crisp edge under the object and keeps one consistent light direction across the whole system. Ambient shadow: soft and directionless, no offset, 2px blur on the low ramp and 8px on the high ramp. It carries the sense of distance. Neither layer works alone. The key on its own looks pasted onto the surface; the ambient on its own looks blurry and weightless. Sharp and tight reads as close to the surface, large and soft reads as far from it.

> **Info:** Apply shadows as Effect Styles (Shadow/xs–xl) via the Effects style picker, never raw drop shadows. Each style ships two layers, ambient + key, governed by Shadow/Blur/*, Shadow/OffsetY/* and Color/Alpha/Black/10. Role map - xs: hovered rows; sm: resting cards & buttons; md: dropdowns, popovers, tooltips, menus; lg: drawers, bottom sheets, sticky bars; xl: modals & full-screen overlays. Same elevation = same style.

> **Accessibility:** Shadow conveys elevation only - never the sole cue for state or grouping; always pair with border or colour. Focus indicators use a ≥3:1 ring, not a shadow (WCAG 1.4.11 Non-text Contrast, 2.4.7 Focus Visible). Ensure modals (xl) don’t obscure the focused field (2.4.11).

> **Info:** Not implemented: Fluent also adjusts shadow opacity by surface luminosity (0.2126R + 0.7152G + 0.0722B) so shadows read equally on brand-coloured surfaces. Syntropy has no brand-shadow styles yet, because Color/Alpha/Black/* ships 10/30/50/70 and Fluent's ramp needs roughly 12, 14, 20 and 24 per cent. The low ramp therefore uses Black/10 on both layers and the high ramp steps its key layer to Black/30, which is the closest available split. On saturated surfaces, prefer a border over a shadow until those tokens exist.

Shadow / none

No shadow - flat surface

Page backgrounds, embedded content within a card, anything that shouldn't feel elevated

Shadow / xs

Ambient Blur/XS · Key Blur/XS + OffsetY/XS · Black/10 both · 2 layers

Input rings on focus, very subtle separation, list items hovered

Shadow / sm

Ambient Blur/XS · Key Blur/SM + OffsetY/SM · Black/10 both · 2 layers

Default - cards at rest, dropdown menus, tooltips

Ambient Blur/XS · Key Blur/MD + OffsetY/MD · Black/10 both · 2 layers

Floating action buttons, popovers, sticky elements

## Elevation in Light vs Dark Mode

Elevation works differently in light and dark mode. The shadow scale documented above is a light-mode mechanism - shadows on a dark background mostly disappear into the surface. Dark mode relies on borders and surface tier shifts instead, which means the two modes need different mental models.

### Surface tiers - 3 in light mode, 2 in dark mode

Light mode provides three distinguishable surface backgrounds: bg/base (pure white), bg/surface (faint off-white), and bg/elevated (slightly darker). The eye reads each as a separate surface even though the differences are subtle. Dark mode collapses this - bg/base and bg/surface resolve to the same near-black, and only bg/elevated is meaningfully different. The system effectively has two tiers in dark mode, not three.

Light mode

bg/base

bg/surface

bg/elevated

↑ 3 distinct surface tiers

Dark mode

bg/base = bg/surface

bg/elevated

↑ Only 2 tiers - borders carry the elevation

### Why shadows largely disappear in dark mode

A drop shadow is a darkened area underneath an element - it works in light mode because "darker than white" reads as clear separation. In dark mode, the surface is already near-black. A darker patch beneath an already-dark surface produces near-zero contrast. The shadow either vanishes or becomes a vague smudge that adds visual noise without communicating elevation. ( also you can produce shadows with white light, that’s just wrong)

| Light mode - shadow communicates elevation Shadow / md applied - clear elevation | Dark mode - shadow barely registers Shadow / md applied - barely visible on dark surface |
| --- | --- |

### In dark mode, borders carry the elevation work

Dark mode borders are slightly LIGHTER than the surfaces they sit on - the opposite of light mode where they're darker. This is the only reliable way to communicate the edge of a surface against a near-black background. Always apply border/subtle or border/default to elevated surfaces in dark mode. In light mode borders are optional polish; in dark mode they're structural.

> **Tip:** Practical rules: (1) In light mode, lift cards with Shadow / sm or md - borders are optional polish. (2) In dark mode, lift cards by switching their background to bg/elevated AND adding border/subtle - shadows are mostly cosmetic. (3) Modals and overlays still use shadows in both modes - they have a backdrop that gives the shadow contrast.

> **Warning:** bg/base and bg/surface resolve to the same color in dark mode. This is intentional - there's no readable way to distinguish three near-black surfaces. If a design relies on distinguishing those two in dark mode, the design needs to use a different mechanism (border, position, or different content) to mark the boundary.

### Anti-patterns (Don't do this)

Common effect mistakes that degrade the system.

> **Don't:** Don't use raw hex shadow colors. The Color/Alpha/Black/* primitives exist specifically for shadow color. A hex shadow color breaks theme switching and creates drift.

> **Don't:** Don't apply shadows via the raw "Effect" panel. Use the effect style picker (Shadow / xs through Shadow / xl). Raw shadows are untracked and create silent drift across files.

> **Don't:** Don't mix radius tokens within a single component. A card with radius/md corners and a button inside with radius/lg corners looks broken. Stick to one radius per visual unit.

> **Don't:** Don't invent custom radius values like 6px, 10px, or 14px. The scale is 0/2/4/8/12/16/20/24/full. If those don't fit, the surface type is probably wrong, not the radius.

> **Don't:** Don't use border/error or border/warning as decoration. They have semantic meaning - using them outside of error/warning states confuses users who are trained to recognize those signals.

> **Don't:** Don't add extra shadow layers on top of a style. Each level already ships exactly two, an ambient and a key, tuned to read as one light source. A third layer muddies the elevation hierarchy and breaks the shared light direction.

> **Don't:** Don't rely on shadows alone in dark mode. They'll be invisible against the dark surface. Use bg/elevated + border/subtle for elevation in dark mode instead.

### Why effects matter

Effects are the polish layer of an interface. Two screens with identical content, typography, and color can feel completely different depending on how their corners, borders, and shadows are treated. The difference is the difference between a $50/month product and a $5/month one.

For a fintech product, this polish translates directly into trust. Users associate sharp corners with brutalist authority, generous radius with friendly approachability, soft shadows with calm confidence, and heavy shadows with attention demands. Each token communicates something - even when the user can't articulate what.

Syntropy's effect tokens are intentionally restrained. A small radius scale (11 steps) forces designers to pick recognized values instead of inventing new ones. A small shadow scale (6 levels) prevents the elevation hierarchy from becoming arbitrary. Restraint is the system's job; expression is the designer's job within those limits.

### Choosing the right radius

Radius is the most underestimated decision in interface design. Most designers either don't think about it (everything gets the default), or they fiddle with custom values screen-by-screen (drift). The right approach is to anchor each surface type to a specific radius token and stick to it.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Inputs and buttons - sm (4px) | Tight radius reads as precise, controlled, professional. Bigger radius on inputs makes the interface feel softer but less serious - fine for consumer apps, wrong for fintech. |
| Cards and modals - md (8px) | The default. Soft enough to feel approachable, tight enough to feel structured. Use this everywhere unless there's a specific reason not to. |
| Prominent cards / sheets - lg (12px) or xl (16px) | When you want a surface to feel notably elevated or marketing-grade. Reserve for hero blocks, feature cards, and bottom sheets - don't scatter throughout the interface. |
| Avatars and circular buttons - full | Use radius/full only when the result should be a complete circle. Don't use full on rectangular shapes - at non-square aspect ratios, full becomes a pill shape, which is a different visual choice. |

> **Tip:** Pick one radius token per surface type at the start of a project. If cards are radius/md, every card in every screen is radius/md. Consistency matters more than which specific value you chose.

### Using shadows for hierarchy

Shadows communicate elevation - how far above the page surface an element sits. Higher elevation = more important. A modal sits above a popover sits above a card sits above the page. Match the shadow to the conceptual elevation, not to your aesthetic preference.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| Resting elements - Shadow / sm | Cards at rest, navigation bars, dropdown menus at rest. Subtle separation from the background. |
| Hovered / active elements - Shadow / md | Hovered cards, floating action buttons, popovers being shown. Slightly more prominent to signal interactivity. |
| Overlay elements - Shadow / lg | Modal sheets, side drawers, bottom sheets. Significantly elevated to signal "this is on top of everything else." |
| Modal-scale dialogs - Shadow / xl | Full-screen dialogs that need to feel detached from the page. Use sparingly - overuse makes everything feel heavy. |

> **Warning:** Shadows are a light-mode mechanism. In dark mode they largely disappear - see the "Elevation in Light vs Dark Mode" section above. In dark mode, lift cards by switching their background to bg/elevated and adding border/subtle, not by relying on shadows.

> **Warning:** Don't use shadow as the primary way to communicate hierarchy. Sighted users see shadows; screen reader users don't. If a shadow is the only thing distinguishing a clickable card from a static one, the interface fails accessibility. Pair shadow with explicit affordances - borders, hover states, focus rings.

### Borders done right

Borders are the cheapest way to separate content. They're also the easiest to overdo - every cell, every card, every input wrapped in a 1px border quickly turns an interface into a grid of cages. The Syntropy border tokens are scoped for restraint.

| Col 1 | Col 2 |
| --- | --- |
| border/subtle is the default for separation | Use border/subtle (the lightest token) for almost all borders. It separates content without screaming. Reserve border/default for places that need more presence, and border/strong for genuine emphasis. |
| Don't pair borders with strong shadows | A card with both a visible border AND a strong shadow looks over-defined. Pick one - either the border separates it from background OR the shadow lifts it from the page. Combining both is redundant. |
| Status borders carry meaning | border/success, border/warning, border/error, border/info aren't aesthetic choices - they're semantic. Don't use border/error to make something visually pop. Use it only when the bordered content is actually in an error state. |
| border/focus is required for accessibility | Every interactive element must show a visible focus ring when keyboard-focused. Use border/focus consistently - don't suppress or restyle focus rings just because they're not in the visual mockup. They're mandatory for keyboard users. |

### Anti-patterns (Don't do this)

Common effect mistakes that degrade the system.

> **Don't:** Don't use raw hex shadow colors. The Color/Alpha/Black/* primitives exist specifically for shadow color. A hex shadow color breaks theme switching and creates drift.

> **Don't:** Don't apply shadows via the raw "Effect" panel. Use the effect style picker (Shadow / xs through Shadow / xl). Raw shadows are untracked and create silent drift across files.

> **Don't:** Don't mix radius tokens within a single component. A card with radius/md corners and a button inside with radius/lg corners looks broken. Stick to one radius per visual unit.

> **Don't:** Don't invent custom radius values like 6px, 10px, or 14px. The scale is 0/2/4/8/12/16/20/24/full. If those don't fit, the surface type is probably wrong, not the radius.

> **Don't:** Don't use border/error or border/warning as decoration. They have semantic meaning - using them outside of error/warning states confuses users who are trained to recognize those signals.

> **Don't:** Don't stack multiple shadows on a single element. Syntropy ships one shadow per effect style for a reason - multiple shadows muddy the elevation hierarchy and look amateur.

> **Don't:** Don't suppress focus rings to make designs look cleaner. Keyboard users rely on them. If a focus ring looks visually wrong in a design, the design is wrong, not the focus ring.
